\section{Derivative convention}
Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be an open interval, let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable, and set $y=f(x)$. We follow the usual calculus convention that $f'(x)$ and $\frac{dy}{dx}(x)$ denote the same first derivative. Define the reported derivative by
\[
g(x)=f'(x)=\frac{dy}{dx}(x),\qquad x\in I.
\]
This statement is local to differentiable points of $f$; it makes no claim at a nondifferentiable point.

\section{Gradient definition}
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $f\in C^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$. The vector-valued function $g:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is defined componentwise by
\[
g(x):=\nabla f(x)=\begin{pmatrix}\partial f/\partial x_1\\\partial f/\partial x_2\\\partial f/\partial x_3\end{pmatrix}(x),\qquad x\in\Omega.
\]
Thus $g$ is the gradient of $f$, not an unrelated multiplication of symbols.

\section{Event union}
Let $A$ and $B$ be events in the same probability space, and let $P$ denote its probability measure. The probability of observing at least one event is defined as $P_{\mathrm{any}}=P(A\cup B)$. Inclusion--exclusion gives
\[
P_{\mathrm{any}}=P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).
\]
The common probability space is required for both the union and the intersection in this equation.

\section{First-order uncertainty propagation}
Near the calibration point, temperature depends on voltage through resistance, so the local derivative chain is
\[
\frac{dT}{dV}=\frac{dT}{dR}\frac{dR}{dV}.
\]
For small perturbations with independent voltage and resistance-calibration errors, first-order propagation gives
\[
\sigma_T^2\approx\left(\frac{dT}{dV}\right)^2\sigma_V^2+\left(\frac{dT}{dR}\right)^2\sigma_{R,\mathrm{cal}}^2.
\]
The approximation sign is an operator in the relation, not a symbol requiring a declaration. No distributional model is stated, so this calculation does not establish a Gaussian confidence interval.

\section{Faraday sign review}
The electric field $\mathbf E(x,t)$ and magnetic field $\mathbf B(x,t)$ belong to the same time-dependent model, with $t$ as the independent time variable. The orientation of the loop and surface is fixed by the right-hand rule. A draft proposed the plus-sign relation
\[
\nabla\times\mathbf E=+\frac{\partial\mathbf B}{\partial t}.
\]
Review rejects that proposal under the stated orientation. The adopted relation is instead
\[
\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\frac{\partial\mathbf B}{\partial t}.
\]
The sign conclusion depends on the recorded orientation and is not a free stylistic choice.
